---
title: "Where emissions and growth move together"
subtitle: "And where, surprisingly, they do not"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/_site_helpers.R")
```

If you had to guess which Canadian provinces show the tightest long-run link between
greenhouse gas emissions and economic output, you would probably say the oil producers.
Alberta and Saskatchewan earn their living from carbon-intensive extraction. When their
economies grow, emissions should grow with them.

The data say otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: province-map
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
plot_province_map()
```

Every province's economy grew over these twenty-three years. What happened to their
emissions did not follow suit. Alberta's output rose 82% and its emissions climbed 36%
alongside it; Ontario's output rose 70% while its emissions *fell* 14%. Emissions rose
across the four western provinces and Newfoundland, held flat in Quebec, and fell in
Ontario and the Maritimes. Nothing in those numbers needs a statistics course to read,
and the split they describe is why the oil-producing provinces behave differently in
everything that follows.

The shading is a different question, and a harder one: not whether emissions and output
happened to move the same way, but whether they are *tied* to one another over the long
run. **Ontario is the only province where both methods agree that they are. Alberta and
Saskatchewan are among those where neither finds it.** The two provinces where the
connection between carbon and money seems most obvious to the naked eye are the two where
it is hardest to establish in the data.

## The question

Economic growth, energy use and greenhouse gas emissions are bound together — but how
tightly, and does the answer depend on where you look?

Most of what is known comes from national studies. Canada is treated as one economy, and
a single answer comes out. But Canada is not one economy. A province built on oil sands
and a province built on hydroelectricity and manufacturing have little in common beyond
a currency.

This study asks whether the national answer survives when you look underneath it:
**eleven jurisdictions — ten provinces and Canada as a whole — each tested separately,
1997 to 2019.**

## What it finds

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Three results

**1. The national relationship does not decompose.** A long-run relationship shows up for
Canada as a whole on one test, but not in most of the provinces that make up Canada. The
country's answer is not the average of its parts.

**2. The provinces where you would most expect a link are where it is weakest.** The
likely reason is that Alberta and Saskatchewan's output is driven by oil prices. The 2008
crash and the 2014–16 price collapse moved their GDP violently without moving physical
emissions in step, breaking the statistical relationship even though the physical one is
real. Ontario's path was shaped instead by a coal phase-out completed in 2014 and a long
manufacturing decline — changes that moved emissions, energy and output together.

**3. Emissions do not predict economic growth anywhere.** Not in any province, not
nationally, under every specification tested. This is the most robust finding here.
:::

## How much to believe

Each jurisdiction supplies **23 annual observations**. That is a short series for this
kind of econometrics, and it shows up everywhere in the results:

- The cointegrating rank — the formal measure of how many long-run relationships exist —
  **changes with an arbitrary modelling choice in ten of the eleven jurisdictions**.
- Standard criteria for making that choice disagree completely: one picks the largest
  option almost everywhere, another the smallest.
- Of 77 causality tests, 13 are significant as originally reported. Under a more
  conservative procedure, 3 survive.

```{r}
#| label: lag-sensitivity
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.4
plot_lag_sensitivity()
```

So the fragility is not a footnote. It is part of the finding: **provincial relationships
cannot be read off national estimates, and 23 years of annual data cannot settle them
either.**

## What this is not

This is a study of *statistical* relationships — whether series move together over time,
and whether one helps predict another. It is not a measurement of how much emissions
respond to growth, and "causality" here means predictive precedence in a technical sense,
not physical causation. Nobody doubts that burning fuel emits carbon. The question is
whether 23 years of provincial accounts can show it.
